thread.title: One More Deep Dive Off The Short End

author: The Idea Guide
title: One More Deep Dive Off The Short End
text:
by Daniel Shvartsman
In my 6+ years at Seeking Alpha and my 7+ following the markets closely, I've only been to a couple investing conferences. Both of them were this year. I covered Buscando Valor in early October . And we've already covered the Kase Learning Shorting Conference in a couple places - a recap from our SA Bulls & Bears account, and a Behind the Idea episode where Mike Taylor and I chatted about what we saw.
I'm taking one more article to review the ideas in a little more focus and depth. I don't think there are many other short focused conferences, and it's interesting to be exposed to such consistently contrarian thinking, if you take it as a given that the market will go up over time. That's especially interesting after two straight bumpy months, with doubts rising over whether we are entering a new phase in the market. So here are the ideas that were discussed, with my usual commentary and analysis based on what the SA community has said:
Gabriele Grego, Quintessential Capital Management: "The Black Hole" - Aphria ( APHA ) This was the first pitch and the headliner. I'm not going to rehash the full thesis, as it's been widely covered and responded to , and is available here . The essence is that the authors (Hindenburg Investment Research as well as Grego) suspect the company of misleading investors about its Latin American transactions, to say the least.
The aftermath is worth reviewing. Aphria is, as I type, down 33% since the pitch came out. The stock has bounced up and down, and the company hasn't fully responded to the thesis yet. It has inked a new deal in Paraguay. Nobody has published a fully bullish piece on SA since the initial article came out, but two types of ideas have come out:
Double down: Hindenburg Investment Research came out with another article arguing that the related party dealings and insider advantages go beyond the LatAm deals.
This may be bad but...: Edward Vranic, CFA argues that this is going to bounce around more and that the play now is long. His timing has been good so far, and he's not alone. Citron Research went long APHA as well on a similar bounce. This hasn't persisted so far, but it provides another side of the trade.
Sahm Adrangi, Kerrisdale Capital Management: "A Short For All Seasons" Adrangi's pitch here was short CarGurus ( CARG ). He prefaced it by comparing it to his last Kase pitch, QuinStreet ( QNST ) as another adtech short. But the short case for CarGurus is much more straightforward, and I think it's more compelling.
CarGurus has a relatively undifferentiated product as a site where you can buy cars. It's grown like a tech start-up, i.e. prioritizing revenue growth over profitability, as compared to legacy firms like Cars.com ( CARS ) and Auto Builder, which were owned more by media companies and focused on profitability. That's enabled CARG to grow fast and gain a higher multiple.
But beyond the natural limit to competing on share and questions over the true profitability of the vertical, what I found most compelling was the company's exposure to Google's ( GOOG ) search algorithm, which will require them to spend more on marketing, further squeezing their profitability. I heard a criticism from someone else at the conference that there's no clear catalyst for this to work, but at 9x sales, it seems sort of safe to bet it won't blow out to the upside.
Chris Brown, Aristides Capital: “My Big Fatty Reefer Vetting” Chris Brown's thesis was on Tilray ( TLRY ) and was entertaining, sprinkled with funny photos and weed lingo. Tilray short isn't the most surprising thesis, but I guess this is an example whether it's better to make money than be clever. Also, Brown's work to illustrate the quantitative and technical elements that make TLRY a good short now, when it has blown out in a squeeze before, are really value add. The stock is down 24% since the pitch, so it's starting to play out, but it may be worth further investigation, embedded below:

Notes: Viceroy Research: “Goodwill Hunting: The Alchemy of Creating Profits” Mads Thamsborg, Bodenholm Capital: "A Roll-Up Gone East" I was surprised to see the conference hadn't coordinated to avoid a case where two people pitched the same stock, but I guess there's only so much you can do in advance (and only so many names to short). But here we are, with two Ebix pitches.
Ebix( EBIX ) was a battleground. It was a big winner for bulls, but started to teeter in October, related to an auditor switch (something that came up in both short pitches). Viceroy focused more on the questionable accounting, including growing receivables - a favorite problem with short companies - and opaque structuring of the business. Thamsborg focused more on the underlying business deteriorating, with growth tailing off as compared to what the company has achieved in the past. Roll-ups depend on growth and on leverage, and now is not the best time to rely on leverage. So I find the set-up interesting.
On the flipside, Ebix continues to have a vocal bullish commenting and contributing base on SA. For example, check out the comments on our podcast interview with Thamsborg, starting here . One aftershock of the pitches was that CEO Robin Raina elected to take his pay in stock until the share price triples. On the surfaced, this is good alignment; I guess the shares could be dilutive, but there's a clear incentive for Raina to get shares to be worth more. I would be curious to hear the bears' response to this.
Matthew Earl, ShadowFall Capital & Research: “Arcadis – A Bridge Too Far” There was a good mix of European based ideas. Matthew Earl talks about Arcadis ( OTCPK:ARCVF ), a construction company, which has some wonkiness on their balance sheet and smoothing out on their earnings. Somebody else asked the question, but it seems like all of these construction/engineering companies have problems. Between the reliance on government (and the possible bidding problems that ensue) and the uncertainty of bidding on contracts in advance and then having to develop them, there are lots of opportunities for things to go wrong.
This was also connected to Mark Hiley's pitch, which I'll hit next:
Mark Hiley, The Analyst Research: "Roll-up And Blow-Up: Calling Time On European Carpet Baggers" Hiley focused on the Schuldschein debt market, which is a debt market in Austria for companies that can't raise debt elsewhere. They get paired with individual providers of debt. Needing to go to Schuldschein is a sign that companies are not super credit worthy, even in a climate of super low interest rates in Europe. On the other side, companies in Europe use this debt to roll-up companies, which allows them to deliver predictable earnings growth, leading to attractive multiples.
He didn't deliver a single short idea, but cited three companies that are poised for a turn. Hexagon ( OTC:HXGCF ) trades at 30x free cash flow per his numbers with single digit organic growth. Elis ( OTC:ELSSF ) trades at 25x FCF and went to the Schuldshein market. Eurofins trades at 35x FCF with single digit organic growth and high debt, fueled by Schuldshein debt. So we have three roll-up plays that could come apart. These also seem less fraught with argument than EBIX, which may make them attractive.
Matthew Kliber, Gracian Capital LLC: "Anything But Brilliant" Kliber has bonafides on the short side, having been roped into the Overstock ( OSTK ) suit over a decade ago . His call on Signet ( SIG ) has already worked in light of the company's Q3 report , which on the surface seemed positive. Kliber's case was that the company overreacted to a Q2 full of one-time effects. While I may be too late for that part to be actionable, I think readers interested in SIG should consider Kliber's broader point, which is that the company sold off its financing operations and books. The end result of that is that the people now managing financing around SIG purchases are running the credit book tighter. This would in theory cause a reset in SIG's revenues. The question I have then is whether this is a one-time reset, after which SIG can resume growth (and it is trading at 8x adjusted 2018 EPS), or whether there are more structural issues that will keep SIG from being a viable investment in the long run.
Keith Rosenbloom, Cruiser Capital Advisor: “A Dead Man’s Hand?” This was my favorite idea from the conference. Rosenbloom's pitch was about Michael's ( MIK ), a company that screens as cheap. His point is it's cheap for a reason - the company is not Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ) proof, and is further getting hurt in its framing business, which makes up 33% of its income. There's also a neat asymmetry (as Mike pointed out on our podcast above), where the private equity firms that brought Michael's and own 42% of the company still are looking to sell whenever the stock gets up to $20. We have good authors pitching the other side of the trade, and I haven't done further due diligence yet, but I thought Rosenbloom set this up very well.
David Berman, Berman Capital: “The Wishful Thinking Theory” The Michael's thesis ties well to David Berman's pitch, which was about retail in general. He had three tenets - first, the wishful thinking theory, which is that stocks that are doing poorly are supported by investors convinced it can't get worse. That seems to relate to Michael's directly. Then, he pointed out that Apple ( AAPL ), Amazon, and Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ) make up the bulk of retail growth, and while the retail sector got a boost in mid 2017, driving traditional retail growth rates up to 3-4% (from 1.5-2%), that is unlikely to sustain. That's because of his third tenet, which is that inventory growth divided by sales growth has inched above 100%, and when inventory outpaces sales growth, that means companies are going to have to unload inventory (and conversely that sales are not pulling things along well enough).
(For what it's worth, Berman called out Party City ( PRTY ) as similarly susceptible to Michael's problems).
Berman's takeaways were that Q4 might be good or might be bad for retailers, but after that, things look bad. Carter's ( CRI ), Dick's Sporting Goods ( DKS ), and Target ( TGT ) were names that stood out as potential shorts.
Ben Axler, Spruce Point Capital: “What’s Left to Short After a 10% Market Correction?” One more retail-related idea was Ben Axler's pitch on Weis Markets ( WMK ). This came down to basic numbers - the company is selling products at higher prices than competitors, and competitors are increasingly encroaching on Weis's territory. Axler has pitched this previously, but it continues to persist in the same range and may be worth a look.
Victoria Hart, Pinnacle View Capital: “Bah Humbug” Victoria Hart pitched three ideas, two of them closely related. Cracker Barrel ( CBRL ) was a short based on the company's declining traction with millennials and loss of share to casual restaurants. I was curious about CBRL's corporate governance given its ties to Biglari Holdings ( BH ), but that didn't come up. She then pitched short KB Home ( KBH ) and Pulte Homes ( PHM ). This was interesting because homebuilders have been underperforming for a while, though she pointed out that they peaked ahead of the market last time around. I also liked her point that investors waiting for millennials to buy homes may be waiting a long time - between lower household formation (i.e. less marriage) and a different ethnic make-up in the cohort that correlates with less home ownership, she debunks the idea that millennials will be just like previous generations. I'm not sure whether there is enough meat on the bone for a homebuilder short, but the point is very astute.
Sunny Puri, Anson Funds: "The Apple Doesn't Fall Far From The Tree" Axon ( AAXN ) is similar to Ebix in my view - a battleground, one that appeared to have been a clear win for bulls but that has come back quite a bit over recent months. The bull narrative has been around a shift to subscriptions and recurring revenue over camera footage, but Puri argues that's actually a sign of weakness as the company runs out of room in its core taser line. He also points out management has hair on it, as the current CEO is related to two people who have had securities legal issues. I'd want to dig in deeper here, and Whitney Tilson recalled how he tried to short Taser a decade ago, so this is a story that has stuck around the markets (I did a write-up of an Axon idea on its way up earlier this year).
Dan David, F.G. Alpha Management: "Don't Quit Your Day Job" Dan David's idea also touched on management concerns, in a roundabout way. The idea was related to his talk on making the China Hustle movie as well as running for Congress. His (victorious) opponent's husband runs a company called ASE, a company into which Ideal Bike (8933.TW) sank over $30M. ASE just declared bankruptcy (if I followed the idea properly). Ideal Bike's market cap is around $60M. Ideal Bike's management team also has ties to people who have run afoul of securities law. Put it all together, and this was one of the more compelling pitches.
Anne Stevenson-Yang, J Capital Research: "The Link Between Chinese Online Streaming Sites And Money Laundering" Anne Stevenson-Yang pitched Momo ( MOMO ), and this has also played out quickly . There were some interesting read-acrosses here. Her argument is that the company is sinking a lot of money into an opaque transaction that is not making any money, and that a lot of its content is risqué (streaming videos of young girls) that could run afoul of the regulators. Beyond that, a lot of the company's transactions appear to be circular . And the ultimate catalyst is a tightening of money supply in China, which will crimp revenue growth rates for MOMO and similar companies. The sell-off last week was over downside guidance. Stevenson-Yang's price target is in the high teens, so there's still room for this to play out.
Carson Block, Muddy Waters Capital: “ActivISM Short Selling” Lastly, Carson Block made an impassioned pitch around shorting as a moral duty. Namely, he meant target firms that appear to have fundamental moral problems. He focused on healthcare, where lives are at stake. Insys ( INSY ) and its role in the opioid crisis was an example, as was American Addiction Centers ( AAC ). On a go-forward basis, he pointed out Acadia Healthcare ( ACHC ) and Health Insurance Innovations ( HIIQ ), both of which may be interesting in light of SA coverage and today's news , respectively.
I also thought the nuance about, as Block called it, charcoal and black was interesting. If lives are on the line, this is really bad and should be called out; if it's just a matter of potential consumer abuse - think short cases against World Acceptance ( WRLD ) or Herbalife ( HLF ) - it may be tough to rally a case behind it. There's a degree of moral outrage that is needed to sustain an activism short case, per Block.
***
That wraps the Idea Guide. This is a fill-in for last week's Idea Guide, which never went out. I'll write a regular Idea Guide tomorrow, and then we'll continue with a weekly review of ideas worth your time each Friday for the rest of the year. The Idea Guide is exclusive for Essential and PRO+ subscribers.
If you have any favorite ideas, suggestions, or corrections, comment below or send me a direct message , or email me at daniel@seekingalpha.com . I would love to hear how to make this more useful for you. See you tomorrow.
